Telomerase. A specialized reverse transcriptase that extends chromosome ends, known as telomeres, by repeatedly adding tandem DNA repeats, specifically TTAGGG in humans, using an internal RNA template. It solves the end-replication problem—the inability of DNA polymerase to fully replicate chromosome termini—and is essential for unlimited cell division in germ cells and some somatic stem cells. Telomerase catalyzes the addition of six-base-pair repeats, TTAGGG in vertebrates, to chromosome three-prime ends. It is a ribonucleoprotein complex composed of a protein component called TERT and an RNA template component called TERC or TR. The mechanism employs repeating addition processivity—the enzyme works like a molecular stamp, synthesizing repeats without moving along the chromosome. The RNA component carries the sequence C-A-A-U-C-C-C-A-A-U-C in the three-prime to five-prime direction, serving as the template for reverse transcription. Activity levels are high in germ cells, stem cells, and cancer cells but low or absent in most somatic cells. Telomere shortening by approximately fifty to two hundred base pairs per cell division acts as a replicative clock. Cells enter senescence after approximately fifty to seventy divisions, a limit known as the Hayflick limit. Approximately eighty-five to ninety percent of cancers reactivate telomerase or use ALT, alternative lengthening of telomeres. The end-replication problem arises because DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the five-prime end of the lagging strand after primer removal, causing progressive shortening with each division. Telomerase evolved to reset this clock, allowing certain cell types to divide indefinitely. Most somatic cells have low or no telomerase activity, creating a built-in replicative limit that protects against unlimited growth—a tumor-suppressing mechanism. The discovery of telomerase in nineteen eighty-five by Greider and Blackburn was groundbreaking, revealing how cells could overcome replicative senescence and explaining both normal aging and cancer immortalization.
